Senses.Explanation: In Chan definitions and debates, no-mind is the absence of every mind one can grasp or deliberately manufacture, but it is not insensate blankness. The records state it, negate any person who possesses it, test it in public questions, and dispute whether calling it the Way is already one barrier too many. Huangbo Xiyun defines it flatly: 'No-mind means no mind of any kind at all' (無心者無一切心也), and says, 'Just be no-mind; that is final' (但能無心，便是究竟). He adds, 'Mind is itself no-mind; there is no one who is no-mind' (心自無心，亦無無心者), and warns, 'Using mind to make no-mind makes mind existent' (將心無心，心却成有). Dahui Zonggao distinguishes this from insensate blankness: 'What is called no-mind is not being inertly unaware like earth, wood, tiles, and stones' (所謂無心者，非如土木瓦石頑然無知). He says that only 'on reaching this state is it first called true no-mind' (到得如此境界，方始謂之真無心), rather than mouth-level talk. At his death Huineng answers who receives the teaching eye: 'One with the Way obtains it; one with no mind penetrates it' (有道者得無心者通). Sikongshan Benjing defends 'no-mind is the Way' (無心是道) in court debate. He first says, 'When mind is extinguished, the Way is absent; mind and Way are one suchness' (心泯道無，心道一如), then answers the objection that 'tiles and pebbles have no mind and therefore should also be the Way' (瓦礫無心亦應是道) by tracing mind and object to the absence of any fixed root. This is distinct from the adverbial lack of intent in the second sense.
Senses.Note: The ordinary sense 'unintentionally' is split below. The Chan no-mind family is also tested in encounters: Luopu Yuanan answers why offering to a no-mind man of the Way exceeds offerings to buddhas, and Falan Yuancheng answers 'What is a no-mind man of the Way?' with 'This morning I ate thin gruel; even now I am hungry' (早晨喫薄粥，於今猶覺饑). Yulin Tongxiu raises the corrective verse, 'Do not say no-mind is the Way; no-mind is still separated by one barrier' (莫謂無心云是道，無心猶隔一重關), and extends its one barrier to 'a thousand and ten thousand barriers' (千重萬重). These are different deployments of the same no-mind, not additional referents.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo Xiyun, in (黃檗山斷際禪師傳心法要) (Essential Teaching on Mind Transmission), defines no-mind as no mind of any kind at all.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有遠禪師者。抗聲謂師曰。今對聖上校量宗旨。應須直問直答不假繁辭。只如禪師所見以何為道。師答曰。無心是道。遠曰。道因心有。何得言無心是道。師曰。道本無名因心名道。心名若有道不虛然。窮心既無道憑何立。二俱虛妄總是假名。遠曰。禪師見有身心是道以否。師曰。山僧身心本來是道。曰適言無心是道。今又言身心本來是道。豈不相違。師曰。無心是道心泯道無。心道一如故言無心是道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Sikongshan Benjing, in (景德傳燈錄) (Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), defends 'no-mind is the Way' in court debate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 志明禪師者。問曰。若言無心是道。瓦礫無心亦應是道。又云。身心本來是道。四生十類皆有身心亦應是道。師曰。大德若作見聞覺知之解。與道懸殊。即是求見聞覺知之者。非是求道之人。經云。無眼耳鼻舌身意。六根尚無見聞覺知憑何而立。窮本不有何處存心。焉得不同草木瓦礫。志明杜口而退。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Sikongshan Benjing, in (景德傳燈錄) (Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), answers Zhiming's tiles-and-pebbles objection.

Senses.Explanation: In ordinary lexical use, the word marks an act or correspondence as lacking intent. A precept-case story has two monks report that one unintentionally committed sexual misconduct and the other unintentionally committed killing (一人無心氾淫，一人無心犯殺). A verse comment says that deliberately planting flowers is not as effective as unintentionally planting willows (有意栽花，不如無心插柳). A preface says that earlier words and the writer's own words 'coincided unintentionally' (無心而自合), explicitly denying deliberate copying. These uses name absence of intent in an act; they are a distinct lexical use from the no-mind defined by Huangbo and Dahui.
Senses.Note: Three independent allowlisted sources attest ordinary lack of intent in rule-violation narrative, proverb, and authorship disclaimer. The graph string is identical to the primary Chan-loaded term, but a clean target for either sense cannot cover both referents without vagueness.
